sections.h2: What is the New York mansion tax?
sections.html:
The mansion tax is a 1 percent charge on the sale of a New York residence when the consideration for the whole conveyance reaches $1 million. It sits on top of the regular state transfer tax and is written into Tax Law section 1402-a.

The 1 percent applies to the consideration, or the part of it that belongs to the residential property. Once a sale crosses the line, the tax is computed on the full residential amount, not only on the dollars above $1 million. A $1,200,000 three-family house, for example, produces $12,000 of mansion tax, which is the figure the state's own FAQ publication uses for that case.

For a seller in New York, the practical point is that the tax is normally the buyer's bill, yet the seller can end up answerable for it. That makes it worth understanding before a contract is signed on any home priced near seven figures.

sections.h2: Who pays the mansion tax when a house sells?
sections.html:
The buyer pays the mansion tax. Section 1402-a(b) puts the duty on the grantee, and the Department of Taxation and Finance repeats that on its real estate transfer tax page.

If the buyer fails to pay, or is exempt, the duty shifts to the seller. In that case the liability is joint and several, meaning the state may collect the whole amount from either party.

The other taxes in a New York sale follow a different split, as the table shows.

Who pays each New York transfer tax (source: NYS Department of Taxation and Finance, real estate transfer tax page)
TaxRate or triggerPaid by
Base transfer tax$2 per $500 of considerationSeller
Mansion tax1% when residential consideration is $1 million or moreBuyer
Additional base tax (New York City only)$1.25 per $500 on residential sales of $3 million or more, or other property at $2 million or moreSeller
Supplemental tax (New York City only)0.25% to 2.9% on residential sales of $2 million or moreBuyer

Residential real property is any premises that is or may be used in whole or in part as a personal residence. The statute names three kinds in particular:

  • a one, two or three-family house;
  • an individual condominium unit;
  • a cooperative apartment unit.

The state's Publication 577 adds detail that surprises owners. A seasonal cottage that sits empty or is rented for part of the year is still residential. So is a house the seller never lived in, as long as it is or may be rented to others as a home.

The same publication draws a line at building size. A structure with a store on the ground floor and three apartments above has four units, so it is not a three-family house. A ten-apartment building does not qualify even if the seller lived in one apartment.

sections.h2: How does the $1 million threshold get measured?
sections.html:
The threshold is measured against everything the buyer pays or owes for the property, not only the cash that changes hands. Consideration includes the price, the cancellation of any debt, and the amount of any mortgage or lien, whether the buyer assumes it or takes the property subject to it.

Several rules in Publication 577 decide close cases:

  • No lien deduction. The base transfer tax lets a seller of a one to three-family house subtract a continuing lien, but the mansion tax does not. A condo that sells for $1 million with a $400,000 mortgage assumed is taxed on the full $1 million for mansion tax purposes, while the seller's base tax is figured on $600,000.
  • Seller costs the buyer absorbs count as price. In the publication's example, a $975,000 sale becomes $1,033,500 once the buyer agrees to cover a $58,500 brokerage obligation, and $10,335 of mansion tax follows.
  • Related sellers are added together. Two co-owners who sign separate $500,000 contracts with one buyer are treated as a single $1 million conveyance.
  • Contract assignments are tested separately. A $900,000 contract assigned for $200,000 is treated as two conveyances, each below the line, when the parties are unrelated and the deal was not built to avoid the tax.
  • Mixed use. If a $1.5 million two-family house holds a $500,000 residential unit and a $1 million retail unit, the whole $1.5 million meets the threshold, but tax applies only to the $500,000 residential portion.

sections.h2: What extra transfer taxes apply in New York City?
sections.html:
New York City sales carry two more state taxes, both added from July 1, 2019. They are explained in the state's technical memorandum TSB-M-19(1)R.

The additional base tax is $1.25 per $500, paid by the seller. It applies to residential property at $3 million or more, and to other property at $2 million or more. The supplemental tax is paid by the buyer and applies to residential sales of $2 million or more, at tiered rates on the entire conveyance:

  • $2 million up to $3 million: 0.25%
  • $3 million up to $5 million: 0.5%
  • $5 million up to $10 million: 1.25%
  • $10 million up to $15 million: 2.25%
  • $15 million up to $20 million: 2.5%
  • $20 million up to $25 million: 2.75%
  • $25 million or more: 2.9%

The memorandum works one example through. On a $7 million New York City residence, the seller owes $28,000 of base tax plus $17,500 of additional base tax, $45,500 in all. The buyer owes $70,000 of mansion tax plus $87,500 of supplemental tax, $157,500 in all. The city also levies its own Real Property Transfer Tax, which the Department of Finance says is usually paid as part of closing costs. Ask the title closer for the current city rate on your sale.

sections.h2: When and where is the mansion tax paid?
sections.html:
The tax is due no later than the 15th day after the deed is delivered. Tax Law section 1410 sets that deadline, and it also bars a recording officer from recording the deed until the return is filed and the tax is paid.

For property outside New York City, the parties file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property sits. In the city they file Form TP-584-NYC, and the city's own transfer tax return is built online through ACRIS, the Automated City Register Information System. If a deed is not going to be recorded, the return and payment go straight to the Tax Department by the same 15-day deadline.

Three filing details can slow a closing. When a limited liability company is the seller or buyer of a building with up to four dwelling units, the filing must come with documents naming its members, managers and authorized persons, down to the individuals who own it. Nonresident sellers must compute their gain and pay any estimated income tax due, unless an exemption on the form applies. And the city's transfer tax return must be signed by both seller and buyer, or the one who did not sign may face non-filer penalties.

sections.h2: Which transfers avoid the mansion tax?
sections.html:
Governmental buyers are exempt, and so are transfers made without consideration. The Tax Department lists the nontaxable conveyances on its transfer tax page, and several matter to families selling a house:

  • A transfer by devise, bequest or inheritance is not a conveyance at all, so a house passing under a will or by intestacy does not trigger the tax at that step.
  • A bona fide gift made without consideration and unconnected to a sale is nontaxable.
  • A transfer given in connection with a tax sale is nontaxable.
  • Conveyances to a nonprofit that holds the land for conservation, parks or historic preservation are exempt from the mansion tax in particular.

A foreclosure or a deed in lieu of foreclosure, by contrast, falls inside the definition of a conveyance. An heir who later sells the inherited house at $1 million or more faces the tax on that sale like any other owner.

sections.h2: What should a New York seller check before a contract near $1 million?
sections.html:
Start with the contract language on who pays which tax, since the statute sets a default and the contract can shift the base tax. If the buyer agrees to pay the seller's transfer tax, the consideration grows by that amount, and both the base tax and the mansion tax rise with it.

Then ask the closing attorney or title company three things: whether the property fits the residential definition, whether any seller concession counts as added price, and who will file Form TP-584 and collect the buyer's payment at the table. Because the seller becomes jointly liable if the buyer does not pay, the filing should be confirmed before the deed is delivered.

faqs.q: Does the New York mansion tax apply to a $999,999 sale?
faqs.a: No, the tax applies only when the consideration for the entire conveyance is $1 million or more. Consideration includes assumed mortgages and obligations the buyer takes over for the seller, so a price just under the line can still cross it once those items are added. Related contracts for the same property are also combined.

faqs.q: Can the seller be forced to pay the mansion tax?
faqs.a: Yes, if the buyer does not pay or is exempt. Section 1402-a(b) then puts the duty on the seller, and the liability is joint and several, so the state may collect the full amount from either side. Confirm with the closing attorney that the buyer's payment is made with the return.

faqs.q: Is there a mansion tax on an inherited house?
faqs.a: Not on the transfer to the heir. The Tax Department says a conveyance by devise, bequest or inheritance is outside the definition of a conveyance. The tax can arise when the heir or estate later sells the house for $1 million or more.

faqs.q: How much is the mansion tax on a $1,500,000 house?
faqs.a: It is $15,000, which is 1 percent of the consideration. The state's FAQ publication applies the same 1 percent arithmetic to its examples, including a $1.2 million three-family house. The seller's separate base transfer tax is $2 per $500, and New York City sales add the city and state taxes described above.

faqs.q: Where do I file for the mansion tax?
faqs.a: Outside New York City, file Form TP-584 with the county clerk where the property is located, within 15 days after the deed is delivered. Inside the city, file Form TP-584-NYC, and prepare the city transfer tax packet online in ACRIS. Unrecorded deeds are filed directly with the Tax Department.
